03 · Claims experience and leakage¶

Questions this notebook answers (from the brief): Where are claims outcomes strongest or weakest, and what might explain this? What does the claims experience suggest about frequency, severity, concentration or emerging risk?

Definitions used throughout

  • Claims view: claims_valid from notebook 01 (claims on a real policy with cover live at notification). Invalid cover claims are analysed separately in section 7.
  • Frequency: claims notified in a period divided by policies in force at the midpoint of that period, annualised. Exposure based, not "claims per policy written".
  • Severity: mean incurred per claim. Median shown alongside because the distribution is skewed.
  • Cost per policy: incurred divided by in force policies. This is the KPI I use instead of loss ratio, see the note below.
  • Large claim: incurred above £50k.

A note on loss ratio. Incurred is roughly 8.5 times written premium in this file. For a commercial insurer that would be absurd. For a levy funded flood reinsurance scheme it is by design: ceded premiums are deliberately below risk cost and the levy fills the gap. So loss ratio is not a meaningful KPI here. Frequency, severity and cost per policy are what move the levy requirement and reinsurance spend.

733 valid claims, £17,174,665 incurred | 717 with a notification date
Incurred / written premium = 8.3x

1. Frequency: the headline finding¶

Policies in force have been flat at about 1,650 to 1,700 since mid 2024. Claims have not. Annualised frequency ran at 9 to 14 percent for two years, then 16 percent in the half year to March 2026, then 24 percent in the half year to September 2026. That is roughly double the long run rate on an unchanged book.

1.1 Is it one event?¶

No. A single flood event shows up as one or two months with a spike, concentrated in one or two regions. Here the increase starts in November 2025 and is sustained through to September 2026, with September 2026 the highest month in the file (60 claims). It spans every region and every peril.

1.2 Who and what is driving it?¶

Comparing the last 12 months (Oct 2025 to Sep 2026) with the prior 12 months:

In [4]:
dated = dated.assign(window=np.select([dated.NotificationDate >= "2025-10-01", dated.NotificationDate >= "2024-10-01"], ["last 12m", "prior 12m"], "older"))
def cmp(col, order=None):
    t = pd.crosstab(dated[col], dated.window)[["prior 12m", "last 12m"]]
    t["change_%"] = ((t["last 12m"]/t["prior 12m"]-1)*100).round(0)
    return t.reindex(order) if order else t
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 8))
for ax, (col, order, ttl) in zip(axes.flat, [("Region", None, "Every region is up, 50% to 170%"), ("ClaimType", None, "Every peril is up, including non flood"),
                                             ("FloodRiskBand", RISK_ORDER[:4], "Every risk band is up; Medium has more than doubled"), ("InsurerCode", None, "Seven of eight insurers are up; Beacon (INS005) is flat")]):
    t = cmp(col, order).sort_values("last 12m")
    y = np.arange(len(t))
    ax.barh(y - 0.19, t["prior 12m"], height=0.36, color=viz.MUTED, label="prior 12m (Oct 24 to Sep 25)")
    ax.barh(y + 0.19, t["last 12m"], height=0.36, color=viz.ACCENT, label="last 12m (Oct 25 to Sep 26)")
    for yi, (p, l, c) in enumerate(zip(t["prior 12m"], t["last 12m"], t["change_%"])): ax.text(l + 1.5, yi + 0.19, f"{c:+.0f}%", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=viz.INK2)
    ax.set_yticks(y); ax.set_yticklabels([f"{i}  {names[i]}" if col=="InsurerCode" else i for i in t.index]); ax.grid(axis="x"); ax.grid(False, axis="y")
    ax.set_xlim(0, t["last 12m"].max()*1.25); viz.title(ax, ttl, f"Valid claims by {col}")
axes[0,0].legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8.5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("../outputs/figures/claims_last12.png"); plt.show()

What might explain it. The data has no loss date, no event code, no weather or cause field, and the portfolio mix is unchanged (notebook 02). So the file cannot distinguish between:

  1. a genuinely wetter period with more, smaller flood events (consistent with flat severity and the spread across regions)
  2. a change in cession behaviour: insurers passing more claims to the scheme, possibly including claims that were not ceded before (consistent with Escape of water rising fastest, section 8, and with the early term claims in section 6c)
  3. a reporting change: a backlog release or a new claims feed in late 2025 (would also fit a step change in November)

Each has a different owner and a different action, which is why "find out which" is the first recommendation rather than guessing.

2. Severity: flat¶

Mean incurred per claim is £22k to £25k in every half year; the median £15k to £18k. The increase in cost is entirely a frequency effect. This is reassuring in one sense (no sign of inflation in repair costs) and unhelpful in another (it rules out the easy explanation of one or two very large losses).

3. Where claims cost sits: Very High risk¶

Very High is 21 percent of policies, 35 percent of premium and 50 percent of claims cost. Its frequency is 19 percent against 13 for High and 9 for Medium, and its severity (£36k) is 70 percent higher than High (£21k). The tariff already charges Very High about four times Low, but on this evidence the differential is not steep enough: cost per policy is £7k for Very High against £3k for High.

4. Region: Yorkshire and the Humber and the North West¶

Frequency is highest in Yorkshire and the Humber (15 percent) and the North West (14 percent), lowest in London (9 percent). Yorkshire also has the second highest severity, so its cost per policy (£3.8k) is more than twice London's (£1.8k). Premium share does not reflect this: Yorkshire is 11 percent of policies, 11 percent of premium and 15 percent of claims cost.

5. Council tax band: no clear gradient¶

Unlike the real Flood Re debate about Bands G and H, this synthetic book shows no systematic relationship between council tax band and claims cost per policy. Band C is highest (£3.2k) and Band E lowest (£2.6k), with frequency bouncing between 11 and 15 percent. Band H has the highest frequency (15 percent) but only 238 policies and 35 claims, so that is within noise. I would not build a recommendation on council tax band from this data.

6. Insurer: Oak & Stone and Bluegate cost the most per policy¶

Cost per policy ranges from £2.5k (Beacon, Cedar, Rivermark) to £3.4k (Oak & Stone). Oak & Stone has the second highest severity (£26k) and the highest frequency (13 percent), on the second largest book, so it is the biggest pound contributor. Bluegate is small but has the highest severity (£27k) and the fastest claims growth. Beacon is the only insurer whose claims did not rise in the last 12 months.

6b. The spread of claim values¶

What a claim costs, across all 733 valid claims. The median is £16k and three quarters are under £30k, but the pound value sits in the middle and upper bands: claims between £10k and £50k are 60 percent of all claims and 58 percent of cost. Only 16 claims exceed £100k (12 percent of cost). A typical claim is about 4 percent of the property's sum insured; the correlation between claim size and sum insured is close to zero, so sum insured is not a useful predictor of claim cost in this file.

6c. Early term claims: the sharpest signal in the file¶

A different cut of the frequency rise. For each half year's new policies, what share had a claim within 90 days of cover starting? For two years it was about 3 percent. It was 5 percent for policies written in the half to March 2026 and 7.9 percent for policies written in the half to September 2026. In the latest half, 47 percent of all claims arrived within 90 days of cover start (normally 26 to 36 percent) and 43 arrived within 30 days (normally 5 to 14).

Claims that arrive right after cession are the classic signature of an insurer ceding a policy it already expects to claim, or of a cover start date that does not reflect when the risk really attached. Both are cession behaviour, not weather. It is concentrated: Elmbridge 13.7 percent and Harbour 11.1 percent of their new policies, against Beacon 2.6 and Cedar 2.9. This does not prove the cause, but it tells action 2 where to look first: loss dates for the 92 early claims, and whether the loss pre-dates the cession.

In [12]:
cut = pd.Timestamp("2026-07-08")   # 90 days before the extract, so every cohort has had 90 days to claim
lagd = dated.assign(lag=(dated.NotificationDate-dated.CoverStartDate).dt.days)
rows=[]
for h in HALF_ORDER:
    pc = inf[(inf.Half==h)&(inf.CoverStartDate<=cut)]; k = lagd[lagd.PolicyRef.isin(pc.PolicyRef)&(lagd.lag<=90)]
    rows.append(dict(written_half=h, policies=len(pc), early_claims=len(k), rate_pct=len(k)/len(pc)*100))

7. Concentration and large claims¶

The distribution is skewed but not extreme: the top 10 percent of claims are 34 percent of cost; claims above £50k are about a third of cost; the single largest is £212k. There is no £1m claim and no cluster of very large losses. Large claims per half year track total claims, so the rise is not concentrated at the top.

8. Leakage: claims the scheme may not owe¶

Two groups, analysed on the full claims file (not the valid cover view), because the point is that they should not be there.

8.1 Non flood peril: Escape of water¶

102 claims, £2.36m, 13 percent of all incurred. Not a flood peril. Every insurer submits some, Harbour the most (16 percent of its claims). Rising fastest of any peril: 19 in the latest quarter against a run rate of about 6.

8.2 Claims with no valid cover¶

42 distinct claims, £763k: 12 orphans, 9 on policies cancelled from inception, 27 after cancellation, 1 after expiry (a few fall under two patterns). Concentrated in Harbour, Oak & Stone and Northstar (20 of the 30 attributable).

Together about £3.1m of claims, 17 percent of all incurred, need validating before they are accepted as scheme cost. That is the single most actionable number in the file.

9. Open claims and reserves¶

149 valid claims are open, carrying £1.2m of reserve. Median age 13 months; nearly a third are over two years old. Combined with the £0.6m reserve on closed claims (notebook 01), the reserve position looks stale: a reserve review would either release money or confirm the incurred figure.

10. Takeaways for the story¶

  1. Frequency has doubled on a flat book (9 to 14 percent for two years, 24 percent in the latest half). Sustained since November 2025, every region, every peril, seven of eight insurers. Severity flat. Cause not identifiable from this file. Robust in direction; the number moves a little with the invalid cover and undated exclusions but the doubling does not.
  2. Very High risk is half the cost on a fifth of the policies, with severity drifting up to £40k. The tariff differential may be too shallow. Robust: 1,270 policies, 242 claims.
  3. Yorkshire and the Humber and the North West are the regional hotspots on frequency and cost per policy. Robust on direction, modest samples.
  4. Council tax band tells you nothing in this file. Robust negative finding.
  5. £3.1m (17 percent) of claims cost needs validating: non flood peril and no valid cover. Concentrated in three insurers. The exclusions themselves are certain; whether the money is recoverable depends on loss dates and policy wording the file does not contain.
  6. Reserves look stale on both open and closed claims. Certain that the data is inconsistent; the cash effect is unknown.
  7. Early term claims have nearly tripled: 3 percent of new policies used to claim within 90 days of cover start; it is 7.9 percent for policies written since April 2026, concentrated in Elmbridge and Harbour. The strongest pointer to cession behaviour as the cause. Robust on direction (29 claims on 367 policies in the latest cohort); the cause still needs loss dates.
